newsitem.title: BELGIUM: French left seen constrained by market discipline.
newsitem.headline: French left seen constrained by market discipline.

text.p: The realities of the marketplace, a constraint that virtually all governments have to endure, is expected to prevent a potential French Socialist government from pursuing a radical shift in economic policies.

Although the strong performance by the left in the first round of France's parliamentary elections has prompted jitters on financial markets, most analysts and EU officials on Monday were confident that the thrust of past policies would remain unchanged.
"I'm pretty confident in that if a Socialist government comes to power it will change its rhetoric when it is faced with everyday pressure from the markets," said a senior EU official.

As with the left-of-centre political regime in the United States, and more recently in Britain, economists say there is a common realisation that a return to interventionist policies runs the risk of unleashing a painful market reaction.

A slumping currency, rising interest rates and falling share prices would quickly accompany an abrupt reversal of the liberalisation, privatisation and, particularly for France, pension reform policies, analysts say.
"None of the anti-reformist and old-style collectivist aspects of a Socialist programme have the slightest chance of being implemented," says John Gray, an economist at Britain's Oxford University.

The question for many, however, is how a new government would balance the rigours of the marketplace with the demands of a frustrated populace, one that increasingly sees rising joblessness linked to the bid for a common currency.
On this point few have any precise answers. Most reckon that there would be a natural gravitation towards the centre-right's past positions.
Specifically, on economic and monetary union (EMU), the betting is that the Socialists would want to keep France on course for 1999, the year the euro is scheduled to be launched.

But should the Socialists have to share a considerable amount of power with the Communists, a party deeply hostile to European integration, some worry France's political future would become much less predictable.
"It definitely gives...more cause for concern. It makes the second round more crucial than had been thought before, because the Communist party might have a bigger role," said one EU diplomat.
Another intriguing factor, say analysts, is the international fallout from a French Socialist victory.

With the right having been booted from power in Britain, and opinion polls in Germany showing continued frustration with Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democratic Party, a Socialist win in France could embolden the political left across Europe.
"The really important thing is how this affects the German Social Democrats," adds Gray of Oxford University.
"It's just got to have a knock-on effect in Germany."
Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) on Monday were quick to shower praise on the left-wing showing, saying the result was a clear protest against neo-liberal policies.

"It shows that economic and financial policies which raise unemployment through restrictive budgets and social spending cuts are condemmed to failure," SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine told journalists on Monday.
Yet the difficulty many have in assessing the future prospects of the left in Europe is in understanding what kinds of policies or strategies they would actually promote.

The unrealism of some of their ideas, such as French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin's plan to create 700,000 new jobs -- half in the public sector -- without tax increases, highlights for many economists a dearth of creative thinking.
"If one thing is clear there is no coherent French left policy," said a Frankfurt-based economist. "When pressed on specifics, Jospin comes across very vague."
